# Chapter 10. Bangalore (1947-2010)

In the early 1970s the journalist Janardhan Roye used to see a young engineer named Vinay Deshpande working long hours in a basement. The basement belonged to the Classic Building on Richmond Road in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), and the firm that occupied it was called, in Roye's spelling, Processors Systems India. One evening Roye went down to see him. Deshpande was holding a soldering iron over a circuit board. He looked up, smiled, and explained that he was putting together 'hi-tech firmware, bound for the US'.[1]

Roye wrote the scene down forty years later, in 2013, in an article about how Bangalore had become a technology city. He dated it to about twelve years before the day in 1985 when Texas Instruments' satellite equipment arrived at Sona Towers by bullock cart, the scene with which Chapter 8 opened. He thought Deshpande typical of the engineers of the 1970s, who worked quietly on their own or alongside the government's industrial, defence and science laboratories.[2] It is one man's memory, and it should be read as that. But it makes a point that the rest of the evidence supports. Bangalore was building electronics for American customers before any American software company had an office there.

Chapter 9 ended with a recruitment advertisement of 1991 that invited sixty-four young engineers to start their careers in Bangalore. This chapter asks why the software trade gathered in that city, and what it did to the city and to the people who lived there. The first answer is older than the trade. Bangalore was a city the Indian state had filled with engineers, laboratories and colleges in the forty years after independence. The second answer is a set of decisions by firms, some of them about engineers and some of them about landlords. The third is a policy that made the city's software parks a kind of export enclave, with their own power and their own links to the world. What the enclave did for the rest of Bangalore is the hardest question, and the evidence on it is thinner than it should be.

## The state's city

N.R. Narayana Murthy, the founder of Infosys, gave his own account of the city's origins in an oral history for the Computer History Museum, recorded in Bangalore in January 2020. 'Right from 1947 when we got independence,' he said, 'the government of India decided to locate its defense oriented high-tech companies in Bangalore, which was away from the border with Pakistan and with China.'[3] He added a reason of geography: the city lay about 250 miles from the Arabian Sea and about 200 from the Bay of Bengal, so that a plane coming to bomb it would be shot down first. That was why, in his telling, Jawaharlal Nehru and his cabinet made Bangalore a defence-oriented, high-technology place.[4] This is Murthy's recollection of the rationale, not a documented decision of the cabinet, and it is given here as his.

The institutions themselves are not in doubt. Murthy named the Electronics and Radar Development Establishment (LRDE), a defence laboratory; Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL); and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). His interviewer added the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), and Murthy agreed that space research came 'in the late '70s'.[5] A social scientist studying the city's poor, Supriya RoyChowdhury, describes the same city from another angle. In the decades after independence Bangalore was known as 'a garden city of retirees' bunglows [sic], and for a significant public sector presence', with central and state government enterprises set up from the early to mid-1950s and 'premier scientific research institutions' founded by the central government. 'The city's development in the first four decades was closely aligned with the development of the state sector,' she writes.[6]

The city's growth followed the same timetable. A research group at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) reports on its website that Bangalore's population grew by 76 per cent between 1971 and 1981, a rise it attributes to the public-sector industries and defence establishments of the 1970s. Between 1991 and 2001, the decade of the software boom, growth was 38 per cent, and the urban agglomeration's population at the 2001 census was 5.7 million.[7] These are the group's figures, not the census tables themselves, but the direction matters. Software did not make Bangalore big. It arrived in a city that the public sector had already made large and full of engineers.

The private technology community grew inside that public one. Vijay Chandru, a former professor of computer science at IISc who later founded a life-sciences company, told Roye: 'Bangalore was a tech city well before the arrival of the MNCs (multi national corporations)'.[8] He called it 'the original Beantown', after Boston, and said that from the 1960s 'a host of engineers were engaged in creating hardware and software solutions' for avionics, defence, telecommunications and weather forecasting, mostly in the public sector.[9]

The education half of the story sits in the same institutions. When Wipro, then a maker of vegetable oils, decided to make computers in 1979, its research team worked inside the Indian Institute of Science's Digital Systems Lab, on equipment the institute could import more easily than a company could, and several of its first employees had trained there; Chapter 5 tells the story.[10] The computer business of a company that later sold programmers to the world began in a university laboratory.

## A flat in Pune

The software trade did not start in Bangalore. Richard Heeks of the University of Manchester, who studied the industry from the late 1980s, wrote in 1998 that it began in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995), 'in the business district around Nariman Point in the late 1970s'. When prices and commuting times rose, part of the industry moved north to the Santa Cruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ), and Bombay remained the centre of the trade 'until at least the mid-1980s'.[11] Then its firms began to run short of people, partly because programmers were leaving for jobs abroad, and the city's high prices and poor quality of life told against it. Firms, foreign investors and would-be founders began to compare Bombay with other places.[12]

Murthy's account of one such comparison turns on housing law. Infosys was founded in Pune in 1981. 'We pretty soon realized that Maharashtra was not the best place to have a startup,' he said, because of the state's tenancy laws.[13] A tenant who had lived in an apartment for seven years could not be made to leave and could claim it as his own. 'With the result, most landlords in Maharashtra refused to give an apartment on rent because of this fear. Unless you were a big company, unless you gave some big bank guarantee, etcetera, etcetera. But no startup could do that.'[14] The founders wanted a state where the law was 'fair between the landlord and the tenant', and Karnataka was one. So the choice narrowed to Madras (Chennai since 1996), in Tamil Nadu, or Bangalore.[15]

They chose Bangalore, Murthy said, 'because of the availability of engineering talent'. Part of the reason was the defence public sector. The other part was education. In the 1970s and 1980s, he said, 'when there were very few engineering colleges in the country, Karnataka had a disproportionately higher percentage of engineering talent and engineering students in the country.'[16] He gave no year for the move, and the date has not been found in a primary record. A later study put the regional supply in numbers. Writing in 2001 for a Stanford University conference on India's economy, the scholar of Silicon Valley AnnaLee Saxenian reported a finding that 60 per cent of India's computer science graduates came from three southern states, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and that the industry was concentrated there 'largely because of their concentration of engineering manpower'.[17] The private engineering colleges described in Chapter 7 were part of that supply.

## Beer, climate and perception

A common answer to the question of why Bangalore won is that companies liked the weather. The evidence makes this partly true but incomplete. Heeks gave the most systematic answer, using a model of how software firms choose locations. He found three factors at work in the mid-1980s and a fourth that took over later.[18]

The first was labour. Bangalore was seen to have 'abundant labour that could be drawn from its long-standing research laboratories, educational institutes and public sector electronics firms', among them IISc and the Indian Institute of Management.[19] The second was quality of life. Bangalore had a reputation 'for a good climate and social life', and IT workers were quickly drawn into the city's social life and its 'pub culture'. Heeks recorded a semi-serious club of senior industry managers, the Beer-drinkers Association of Information Technology, whose members met to discuss strategy on condition that each drank at least six mugs of beer in the evening. Bombay, by contrast, had 'a long and troubled history of both communal and labour relations strife'.[20] The third was infrastructure. 'You could get across town in a matter of minutes in a car,' where Bombay's peak-hour traffic could take hours, and Bangalore promised plentiful power and water.[21]

Heeks added a caution that applies to every account of why industries cluster. From his interviews, 'the perception of these factors as much as their reality has coloured locational decisions'.[22] Climate, then, was real, but it was one element in a perceived quality of life. C.S. Murali of IISc, quoted by Roye in 2013, gave the weather more weight. He listed a liberalised economy, friendly state policies, a skilled English-speaking workforce and the public-sector giants, and then, 'above all', the city's 'inviting salubrious climate and cosmopolitan character'.[23] Murthy's account of why Infosys moved does not mention the weather.[24] Asked later in the same interview what had made Bangalore a technology hub, however, he began: 'First of all, Bangalore has had a pretty salubrious climate.' Engineering talent came second.[25] So two insiders rank the climate high, but neither gives it alone, and both name skilled people too. Heeks's interviews and Murthy's account of the Infosys move put engineers first. Climate was a real and perceived amenity that made the city easier to sell to engineers and managers. As the main reason for Bangalore's rise, the climate story is mostly false; as one reason among several, it is true.

The infrastructure advantage was the least durable of Heeks's factors. By 1998 a rival city was already advertising Bangalore's traffic as its weakness, as the section on Hyderabad below shows. By 2005 Saxenian reported that the concentration of technology production had brought 'rapidly rising wages and intensifying congestion', and that engineering salaries in Bangalore were 'now among the highest' in India, yet firms kept clustering there rather than moving to cheaper places.[26]

## Twenty-five rules

Heeks treated the arrival of Texas Instruments (TI) as 'a key event in Bangalore's history'. Once TI 'set up operations in 1986, it was the first proper offshore software facility, using satellite-based telecommunication links, and this was constantly reported in the home and international media'. The company was also 'known to have cut through many red tape barriers, particularly on imports'. From then on, he wrote, the Bangalore 'snowball effect' began.[27] Chapter 8 tells how the link was negotiated and weighs the sources' dates for it, 1985 or 1986.

Saxenian put a number on the red tape. Citing an interview given in 1996 by N. Seshagiri, a former additional secretary in the Department of Electronics, she wrote: 'When Texas Instruments set up the first earth station in Bangalore in 1986, for example, the process involved removing or breaking 25 different government rules.'[28] Without such links, she added, Indian firms 'had no alternative to providing contract programming on-site', at the customer's premises and usually in the United States.[29]

Other multinationals followed TI, and they explained themselves in terms of skill and risk. One American employer in Bangalore, in an interview of 1996 cited by the researcher Balaji Parthasarathy and quoted by Saxenian, said: 'we came here because of the skills. We expanded because of the skills.' The risks of distance, of the satellite link, the telephones and the flights, 'were offset by the costs'.[30] A second passage in Saxenian, quoted in Chapter 15, has the chief executive of an offshore development centre claiming parity with his company's headquarters in Silicon Valley; her footnotes trace both passages to the same interview of July 1996, so they may be one man.[31] The manager is anonymous and speaks through two layers of citation. His words are evidence of what managers said, not of what the work was.

Some of the work was hard engineering. TI's Bangalore centre began by designing tools for chip design. Its engineers went on to design a digital signal processing chip, announced in 1997 under the code name Ankur, Sanskrit for seedling, which V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, says was designed entirely in India and widely used in disk drives and instruments.[32] Saxenian noted that the chip had 'become a standard'.[33] Oracle opened a software development centre in Bangalore in 1994.[34]

By 1998 the snowball could be counted. A Dataquest survey of 558 Indian software companies, reproduced by Heeks, found 152 with headquarters in Bangalore, against 122 in Bombay, 93 in Madras, 86 in Delhi, 34 in Hyderabad and Secunderabad, 27 in Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001) and 22 in Pune.[35] Heeks warned that the table understated Bombay, which was still home to several of the largest firms. But since the mid-1980s, when Bombay had led on numbers, Bangalore had grown at its expense and had come to be called India's 'Silicon Plateau'.[36]

## The parks and the bargain

The state that had built Bangalore's laboratories now built its export infrastructure too. Chapter 8 told how the Software Technology Parks (STPs) began. Bangalore's opened in October 1990.[37] An STP, Saxenian explained, was 'like an export processing zone for software'. Firms in it received five years' exemption from tax, guaranteed access to high-speed satellite links and reliable electricity, ready office space, duty-free imports of equipment and permission for full foreign ownership, 'in exchange for a sizable export obligation'.[38]

The obligation is worth reading closely, because it states the bargain plainly. A park firm had to earn, net, 150 per cent of the value of its imported hardware within four years, and 'a net amount equal to 150% of their wage bill on an annual basis'.[39] The second rule meant that a firm's Indian payroll had to be earned back one and a half times in exports every year. From January 1995 park firms could sell a quarter of their output in India, and from 1999 half.[40] The local directors of the parks were meant to act as 'friend, philosopher and guide' to the industry.[41] By 1998 the scheme had spread to 25 parks at various stages of planning, besides the government's own, and some were private ventures. The Information Technology Park in Bangalore, Saxenian noted, was a partnership of the Karnataka government, Tata Industries and a consortium of Singapore firms.[42]

The parks moved work from America to India, slowly. The share of Indian software exports earned at clients' sites abroad fell through the 1990s but was still more than half in 1998; Chapter 9 sets out and compares the series.[43] By 1995, 435 companies were registered under the scheme, accounting for more than 16 per cent of exports.[44]

Karnataka's numbers grew fastest. According to the state's development report of 2007, cited by RoyChowdhury, the number of software export companies in Karnataka rose from 13 to 1,154 between 1991 and 2003, and the state's software exports from Rs 5.6 crore (Rs 56 million, about $2.5 million) to Rs 12,350 crore (Rs 123.5 billion, about $2.65 billion).[45] In the second half of the 1990s Karnataka was, she writes, the only state to grow faster than 8 per cent a year.[46]

## What the work paid

The economics behind the cluster were simple, and Saxenian set them out without ornament. 'India's greatest asset is a large, educated, English-speaking workforce that is willing to work at relatively low wages.' In 1994, she wrote, 'wages for software programmers and systems analysts in India were less than one-tenth of those for their US counterparts, and lower even than other developing countries like Mexico'.[47]

Low wages meant low revenue per worker. On the figures Saxenian used, the industry employed about 180,000 people in 1998 (other counts differ, as Chapter 9 shows), and annual revenue per employee was $15,000 to $20,000, against about $100,000 per employee in Israel and Ireland.[48] Wages rose fast from their low base: the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, estimated that software pay rose 21 per cent a year in the late 1990s.[49] That eroded the cost advantage that had brought the work. Ashank Desai, chairman of Mastek, which Saxenian called a leading Indian software company, said in 1999 that Indian firms were finding it 'difficult for them to compete only on one differential', which was cost.[50] The largest firms, among them Wipro and Infosys, were seeking bigger contracts, often on a turnkey basis, in which the firm delivers a finished system. 'Rather than competing on the basis of hourly productivity,' Saxenian wrote, 'they aim to accumulate intellectual property.'[51]

For the programmers, the city was often a waiting room for America. Those who worked abroad for Indian firms were, in Saxenian's account, 'paid their salaries in rupees and provided with minimal allowances for housing and expenses', and some called the business 'resume selling'.[52] 'Many thus aspire to work for foreign companies,' Saxenian wrote, 'not only for the relatively high wages but also for the opportunity be transferred overseas.'[53] By 1999 Indians were receiving the largest share of the H-1B temporary work visas that the United States issued, a story Chapter 13 takes up.[54]

Behind them came a large training system. Saxenian, citing Nasscom, reported that Indian colleges and polytechnics trained more than 67,000 computer science professionals a year, and that 'another 200,000 individuals enroll annually in the private software training institutes that have mushroomed in India in the 1990s'.[55] The quality of that training is the subject of Chapter 12. What matters here is that Bangalore drew on it and on the colleges of the three southern states that supplied most of the country's computing graduates.

The gap between those who got the jobs and everyone else stayed wide. Writing in 2013, Roye reported that the average software professional in Bangalore, outside the call-centre trade, earned Rs 50,000 a month, which he put at about $1,000, more than eight times the state's monthly income per head of Rs 6,000.[56] He did not give a source for the figure, and it is a journalist's estimate. But it is consistent with the direction of Saxenian's evidence a decade earlier: fast-rising pay for a skilled minority in a poor state.

## Cyberabad

In November 1998 the chief minister of the neighbouring state of Andhra Pradesh, the 48-year-old Nara Chandrababu Naidu, inaugurated a building called CyberTowers near Madhapur, on the edge of Hyderabad. It was to be the centrepiece of a planned Hi-Tech City. 'Until now, the world has heard of the twin cities of Hyderabad-Secunderabad,' he said. 'From today, the world will know of the triplet cities of Hyderabad-Secunderabad-Cyberabad.'[57]

*Business Today*'s cover story the next month, written by an economist based in Hyderabad, set the challenge in context. Hyderabad had once been called the nation's second capital, and public-sector firms such as Bharat Heavy Electricals and the Electronics Corporation of India had set up there in the 1970s. But 'the late 1980s saw Bangalore overtaking Hyderabad' as South India's most dynamic and corporate-friendly city.[58] Naidu's answer was to court the largest names in software. 'When Naidu got Microsoft's CEO, Bill Gates, to locate its R&D centre at CyberTowers, he made sure no other company could ignore the city.'[59] Oracle, BaaN, Tata IBM, Satyam, Wipro and others were already there.[60] This is the magazine's account; Microsoft's own announcements have not been consulted for this book.

Hyderabad's pitch was aimed at Bangalore's weak point. J.A. Chowdhury, a director of the Software Technology Parks of India and, in the magazine's words, a key player in Naidu's Project Cyberabad, put it bluntly: 'Hyderabad is preparing for the future. Other cities will be left behind when traffic-congestion and urban chaos overtakes them.'[61] He described the city as a 'knowledge hub'. It had the first Indian Institute of Information Technology, research institutes, defence laboratories and six universities, so that the supply of computing skills matched the demand.[62] 'Infotech professionals would like to live close to work so that they can work early morning or late into the night,' Chowdhury said, and the magazine added that housing could always be found within ten minutes of the workplace.[63] The magazine, making Naidu's case, also cited a Nasscom survey of IT professionals that scored Hyderabad 3.40 out of 4 for the availability of qualified people and 3.20 for quality of life, but only average for climate, commuting and its educational facilities.[64]

The same article recorded doubts. Drinking water was short. Large parts of the city had 'grown haphazardly'. V.K. Bawa, one of its best-regarded urban planners, had drawn up a plan in the 1970s that no government had implemented, and he complained: 'The model of Hyderabad's development is regressive; it does not conform to modern concepts of urban growth.'[65] The whole project depended on one politician. If Naidu won the next state election, due in November 1999, the direction was clear. 'If he loses, the imponderables are many.'[66]

Saxenian saw in Naidu something larger than one city's ambition. While the central government had begun liberalisation, she wrote, 'the state governments have pioneered some of the most far-reaching policy innovations in the IT sector', and Naidu had made 'e-governance', the use of computers to deliver public services, his signature.[67] His campaign set off competition from his neighbours. Karnataka's new government announced plans to upgrade its 'overburdened roads', and Tamil Nadu and Kerala drew up IT policies of their own.[68] By 2001 software employment was concentrated, in her words, in Karnataka (Bangalore), Andhra Pradesh (Hyderabad), Tamil Nadu (Chennai), Maharashtra (Bombay) 'and areas surrounding Delhi'.[69] The histories of Pune, Chennai and the Delhi region in these years are not documented in the sources gathered for this book, and they are not guessed at here.

## The enclave

The sharpest contemporary warning about the cluster came from Saxenian herself, in a paper whose title asked whether Bangalore was 'the Silicon Valley of Asia'. Her answer was that the comparison was 'not only misleading but also distracts attention from the deeper challenges and opportunities that IT affords the Indian economy'.[70] Silicon Valley had grown with a large home market, an educated population and working infrastructure. Bangalore's future, she wrote, depended 'either on continued supplies of low cost of skill or on shifting into higher value-added activities', and comparisons with California 'remain premature at best'.[71]

The parks worked because they were sealed off from the country around them. 'Already most IT development occurs in STPs that are insulated from the day-to-day challenges of doing business in India by dedicated communications links, private power sources, and liberal rules for investment and taxation.'[72] The insulation was a response to real shortages. In 1997 India had 18.6 telephone lines per 1,000 people, against 55.7 in China, and a new connection took more than twelve months to arrive.[73] In 1997 there were 2.1 personal computers per 1,000 Indians.[74] Her 2005 paper made the same point about entrepreneurs: in India they relied 'on private telecommunications facilities and power supplies rather than on the nation's costly and unreliable infrastructure'.[75]

The cost of insulation, she argued, was disconnection. 'Professionals in IT enclaves could become better connected, both economically and socially, to distant regions than to the rest of the Indian economy.'[76] She cited warnings of 'Dutch Disease', in which dollars from a narrow sector, IT being under 1 per cent of GDP, push up the rupee and hurt other industries.[77] And she put the paradox in one sentence: 'Indian workers today are contributing to the development of software to modernize foreign governments and corporations while their counterparts at home remain woefully backward.'[78] The current policy, she concluded, 'risks accelerating the growth of IT as a small, modern enclave in a poor and backward economy'.[79]

## The road not taken

Saxenian did not think the enclave was the only possible Bangalore. India, she wrote, 'already has the design capabilities' to build products of its own, visible in the chip-design work of the foreign development centres and in small local firms such as Silicon Automation Systems and Encore Software. 'However India lacks the environment needed to support experimentation with the application of these skills to new markets.'[80]

Her example was the Simputer, a very low-cost mobile personal computer priced at under Rs 9,000, about $200 by her conversion, built by a Bangalore team drawn from IISc's Department of Computer Science and Automation and Encore. It ran on the free Linux operating system, was 'designed to be open and modular', and carried a smart-card reader for financial transactions. The collaboration between a public institute and a private firm, she wrote, was 'rare in India'.[81] Encore, Rajaraman records, was the company of the same Vinay Deshpande whom Roye had seen with a soldering iron on Richmond Road in the 1970s.[82] Saxenian also drew on remarks by Ashok Jhunjhunwala at a Bangalore conference in December 1999, who argued that a pager sold in India for Rs 2,200 could be made locally for Rs 100 and so be affordable to a fifth of the population.[83]

Her prescription was a level field: 'IT products and services sold domestically' should 'enjoy the same tax benefits as those currently enjoyed by software export units'.[84] That sentence describes, from Bangalore, the logic this book has followed since the 1970s. A tax and infrastructure regime built to earn foreign exchange made it easier to sell software abroad than at home. The structure of the industry reinforced it. Ten firms earned more than half of all software exports, out of 826 exporting companies.[85]

## K.S. Garden

What did the boom do for the people of Bangalore who did not write software? The most careful answer in the sources comes from RoyChowdhury's study of six slums in the inner city, on J.C. Road close to Lalbagh, which she calls the central commercial hub of the city. She surveyed 300 households and held focus groups; the paper, published by Oxford University's Contemporary South Asian Studies Programme, is undated but was released around 2011.[86] She begins with the transformation. The city had 'become the icon of India's information technology revolution'. Real estate prices soared. The large campuses of the public-sector firms became 'shadows of a past': much of their land was put up for sale, units closed, and their permanent workforces were 'downsized and contractualized'.[87]

The new economy grew, she writes, 'through the expansion of capital intensive rather than labour intensive industries, as well as skill-based industries, which offered limited scope of employment, and only to technically skilled personnel'.[88] The poor found work in construction and in the export garment trade, at low wages, and in new service jobs: driving the cars and vans of call centres and outsourcing firms, guarding and cleaning malls and supermarkets, waiting at tables. Whether in factories or services, that work remained 'in the casual/contract mode with no security of service, insurance or pension'.[89] 'In Bangalore, nearly one million poor live in slums,' she reports, and about a third of slum dwellers lived below the poverty line, on less than Rs 2,500 a month, which she converts as $55.[90]

The IT economy reached one of her slums, K.S. Garden, in a particular way. It had the lowest poverty ratio of the six. Families in its better-paid occupations, from skilled trades to permanent jobs in public bodies, could send their children to private English-medium schools or to computer training.[91] 'About 50 youths in the slum had managed to get some kind of computer training. Of these, some 25-30 women were working as receptionist in small offices, or showrooms, at cash counters in small super markets.'[92] They had left the low-paid work of their parents. But the gain was fragile. In the focus groups, 'even those with some computer training frequently remained unemployed or only partially employed', and where someone had found a foothold, 'a connection through family or network had worked in most cases'. RoyChowdhury's conclusion is plain: 'there had not been any systemic or policy based effort to incorporate the urban underclass into the city's growing economy'.[93] In the same slum, coolie labour and domestic service still accounted for 52.3 per cent of households surveyed.[94]

These are collective voices, reported by a researcher. Roye's article of 2013 names two individuals, both young women from the villages and towns around the city. Anusaya, from Immadihalli village, worked at an ice-cream kiosk in a shopping mall in Whitefield, one of the new technology districts, for Rs 6,000 a month, about $100 by Roye's conversion. 'I work here in the day, go to evening college,' she told him. 'The money I earn meets some of my family expenses and funds college fees.'[95] Ramya Gowda, from Malur, worked at a doughnut counter. 'I got this job because I learnt English and have finished school,' she said. 'This is a part time job. I'd like to study more, especially computers, and work in a big company like Yahoo!'[96] Neither was a software engineer. Both were working at the edge of the economy that software had built, and both described education, English first and computers next, as the way in.

Roye recorded what the corridors had replaced. The campuses of Whitefield, Electronic City and the Outer Ring Road stood largely on what had been farmland or swamp; many farmers on the city's edge had sold their land; the city had fewer trees, lakes and open spaces, and was by his account the third most expensive in India.[97] He ended the article in a bar on Lavelle Road, where a young software worker from Thanisandra told him: 'Seriously uncle, the city has arrived!'[98]

## Three readings

The evidence supports three readings of what happened in Bangalore, and they are not exclusive.

The first is a story of agglomeration. A city filled with public-sector engineers and laboratories attracted a few early movers, TI, Wipro and Infosys among them, and the cluster fed itself as employees left to found firms nearby.[99] On this reading Bangalore's software industry was the delayed return on forty years of state investment in defence, science and engineering education.

The second reading is Saxenian's, that Bangalore was not and could not quickly become a Silicon Valley. It depended on cheap skill and an export regime, and its best engineers were drawn towards America.[100] The evidence of TI's chip, and the offshore managers' claims of parity (Chapter 15), shows the capability was real. The evidence of revenue per worker shows how little of it was being used.

The third reading is about the city. The industry created a well-paid professional economy with private power, private links and few ties to the city's poor, who found work driving its vans and guarding its malls.[101] The two urban histories that would test this reading most fully, Janaki Nair's history of twentieth-century Bangalore and James Heitzman's study of its planning in the IT era, have not yet been read for this book, and neither have the ethnographies of Bangalore's software workers. Until they are, the professionals' own account of their city is missing from this chapter.

What filled the parks at the end of the 1990s was routine work done at great volume: hundreds of American and European companies, Saxenian wrote, outsourced 'coding, maintenance and Y2K solutions' to Indian firms.[102] The next chapter follows the two things that made the late 1990s the trade's boom years: a deadline at midnight on 31 December 1999, and the opening of American stock markets to Indian software firms.

# Chapter 11. Y2K and Nasdaq (1995-2002)

At twenty past six on a Tuesday morning in late 2000, a correspondent for *Business Today*, R. Sukumar, stood on a street in BTM Layout, a growing neighbourhood in south Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), opposite a restaurant called Udipi Garden. He was waiting for a company bus. It was one of the buses that carried close to 4,000 people a day to the campus of Infosys Technologies on Hosur Road, and he had been told that many of its staff lived nearby. Staff from outside the south, he learned later, often clubbed together in threes or fours to sub-let a flat or house in neighbourhoods like this one.[1] On the bus, almost everyone was young and almost nobody talked. People read newspapers, one young woman read what looked like a technical book, and a few at the front fell asleep. The company discouraged its junior staff from riding motorcycles to work, because Hosur Road was so dangerous.[2] The crowd was more mixed than he had expected: many from the south of India, as he had assumed, but also faces from the west, the north and the north-east.[3]

The bus reached the campus at a quarter past seven. Sukumar had visited in the summer of 1995, when it had one office block, one canteen and one small gymnasium. Now it covered 50 acres and had five office blocks, three canteens, a branch of the old Bangalore eating house Mavalli Tiffin Rooms, a coffee bar, a pizza outlet, a swimming pool, a sauna, a medical centre and a small golf green.[4] It also had a three-storey training centre, built for Rs 23.6 crore (about $5 million), where every batch of new engineers went through a three-month course. The whole campus, the magazine reported, would eventually cost Rs 320 crore, about $71 million. Its chief financial officer, T.V. Mohandas Pai, showed off a building whose curved walls, he said, had taken more than 4,000 equations to get right.[5] The cars that drove in a little before eight were mostly small Marutis and Santros. Everyone paid market prices for food in the canteens.[6]

The magazine had named Infosys the best employer in India, and its article was written in that spirit.[7] But its numbers were specific. The share price had risen from Rs 63.75 in early April 1996 to Rs 7,160 on 15 December 2000. Of the company's 7,925 employees at the end of September 2000, 7,853 had been offered stock options, creating, the magazine reported, '1,773 rupee millionaires and 213 dollar millionaires'.[8]

Five and a half years earlier this firm had walked out of a negotiation with its largest customer and lost a quarter of its business. This chapter is about what happened in between. It covers the years when the leading Indian services firms turned a way of organising work into something they could certify, sell and list on an American stock exchange; when a programming error in old American software, the millennium bug, brought them inside the largest companies in the United States; and when the market that had made their employees rich turned and fell. It is a chapter about a business model. It is also about the young engineers on that bus, how they were chosen and trained, what they were paid, and what happened to the graduates who came after them when the boom broke.

## A quarter of the revenue

Chapter 9 told the story of May 1995 from the oral history of N.R. Narayana Murthy, the company's co-founder: when General Electric (GE), then about a quarter of Infosys's revenue, sought lower prices, Infosys alone among its Indian suppliers refused, in Murthy's telling, and handed its GE work to competitors. As he recalled it in 2020, a cut for GE would have meant cuts for every other client, and less money for pay, tools and training.[9]

Two lessons can be read in the company's later filings. The first was about dependence. When Infosys registered its shares with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in February 1999, its largest client provided 10.5 per cent of revenue in the year to March 1998, and it had about 130 clients.[10] The same document listed among the causes of uneven results 'the size, timing and profitability of significant projects'.[11] By the year to March 2002 the largest client provided 6.1 per cent of revenue and the five largest together 24.1 per cent. In both filings the company described its mix of work as chosen 'in an effort to avoid service or client concentration'.[12] The second lesson, in Murthy's own account, was about price. He said in 2020 that 'at least until 2007, 2008, probably 2009, Infosys always got 20-25 percent higher price compared to our competitors in India'. He credited a sales method the company called Business Value Leverage, which meant talking to clients about what the work would be worth to them rather than about technology.[13] No independent price data have been found to test the claim. It is the founder's.

What the filings do show is how fast the firm grew from its small base. Revenue rose from $9.5 million in the year to March 1994 to $68.3 million in the year to March 1998.[14] Over the same years the number of its IT professionals rose from about 480 to about 2,200, and its development centres in India from two to nine.[15] Revenue grew at a compound rate of 63.6 per cent a year.[16]

Part of that growth came from the currency. In the year to March 1998, 90.0 per cent of Infosys's revenue was earned in US dollars, and the filing said that 'a significant portion' of its costs, including pay, would continue to be in rupees. Between December 1994 and December 1998 the rupee lost about 39.5 per cent of its value against the dollar.[17] A firm that earned dollars and paid rupees gained from every fall in the rupee unless it raised salaries to match. Process, Y2K and good management all contributed to the margins of these years. So did the exchange rate.

## Selling the process

To sell work that would be done ten thousand miles from the client, the firms had to show that it would be done properly. They sought two certificates. The international quality standard ISO 9001 was awarded after auditors inspected a firm's documentation, testing and project methods, and the Capability Maturity Model (CMM) of the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) at Carnegie Mellon University graded the 'maturity' of a firm's development process on five levels.[18] In the account of V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, ISO 9001 certification was 'essential for bidding for software projects in Europe whereas the CMM maturity level is valued more in the USA'.[19]

The race to the top level began with a claim that is still unconfirmed. Motorola's Global Software Group, which was set up in India in 1991, says in its own press material that its Indian centre reached Level 5 in 1993 and was 'the first commercial organization in the world' to do so.[20] Rajaraman repeats the claim without a separate source.[21] A *Business Today* report, which this book has not seen, is recorded in its source notes as saying only that Motorola was the first in India, and as dating it to 1994. No record from the SEI itself has been found, so the claim is Motorola's.[22]

By the end of the decade Indian firms held a large share of the highest ratings, though the sources do not agree on how large. The researcher AnnaLee Saxenian, writing in 2001, said that in December 1999, 137 Indian companies had ISO 9000 or CMM Level 2 certification, 'and ten companies were certified at Level 5 (the highest level, at which only six U.S. companies are certified.)'[23] Rajaraman gives a different figure for the same year: 'In 1999, 6 out of 12 CMM level 5 certified companies in the world were in India.'[24] The two counts may cover different months or count organisations differently. Either way, a handful of Indian firms held a large share of the top grade, and the industry said so loudly. 'Quality certification', Saxenian wrote, 'serves as an important marketing device'.[25]

Infosys described its own standing in the February 1999 filing: it had 'been certified at Level 4, a level achieved by only 2% of the more than 1,000 software companies tested under the Capability Maturity Model'.[26] Both the 2 per cent and the word 'certified' are the company's. The SEI's process was an appraisal, and the industry described the result as a certificate.

Rajaraman also explained why process mattered to the firms themselves. Both certificates, he wrote, 'require emphasis on well documented processes which every software engineer in the organization is expected to follow'. And 'The process orientation allowed companies which were recruiting large numbers of employees each year to quickly train them to become productive members of a development team. Staff attrition also could be managed better due to the disciplined software development process.'[27] Rajaraman presents this as a benefit, and it was one. But it also describes what process did to the engineer. A firm that hired thousands of graduates a year, and lost many of them to rivals or to American visas, needed work broken into documented steps that any trained graduate could follow and any other could take over. The certificate reassured the client. The process underneath it made individual engineers easier to replace. That is an interpretation of Rajaraman's words rather than his own conclusion. This book carries the interpretation one step further, and labels it as its own reading: documented, standardised work is also the kind that machines can most easily learn to do. Chapter 19 sets that reading against what the firms' own filings later said about tools for coding, testing and documentation.

## The pyramid

The work itself was organised as a pyramid. Infosys's 1999 filing described a typical project: a 'small team of two to five IT professionals' visited the client to set the scope, then its managers went back to India 'to supervise a much larger team of 10 to 50 IT professionals', with the client's systems 'linked via satellite' to the Indian centres.[28] A few experienced people faced the client. Many junior people did the work in India. The filing said the company did about 80 per cent of its project work in India.[29]

The firm described its own model as an industry practice. 'The Indian offshore development model was initiated in the mid-1980's,' the filing said (Chapter 6 tests that dating against the founders' own careers), and it listed what attracted clients: a large pool of English-speaking professionals, 'relatively low labor costs', international quality standards, the 'capability to work on specific projects on a 24-hour basis by exploiting time zone differences', and the ability to run phases of a project in parallel.[30] By 2002 the language had changed. The annual report for the year to March 2002 said that 'Our clients leverage our proprietary Global Delivery Model to achieve higher quality, rapid time-to-market and cost-effective solutions.'[31] In three years an industry practice had become a company brand.

For the industry as a whole, the move offshore was real but slower than the brand suggests. On each of the series that Chapter 9 compares and reconciles, more than half of the industry's export work was still done at clients' sites abroad, which is why the story of the H-1B visa (Chapter 13) runs alongside this one.[32]

The pyramid was efficient at turning cheap hours into exports, but by international standards it produced little revenue per head (Chapter 10 gives Saxenian's comparison with Israel and Ireland). Saxenian saw the largest firms, such as Wipro and Infosys, trying to escape that trap: winning larger contracts 'often on a turnkey basis', charging higher rates, and turning what they learned on one project into software components they could reuse for the next.[33] The same pages record the other way out. Indian programmers, aware of what their skills earned abroad, were leaving, many of them on the American visas that Chapter 13 follows.[34]

The pyramid had a consequence that a senior Infosys manager described in the *Business Today* article, published in January 2001. Sales had more than doubled in the first half of the year to March 2001, and the magazine noted that growth widened the middle and top of the organisation. 'We are growing so fast that many people with two to three years experience are getting into managerial roles,' said Hema Ravichandar, the senior vice-president for human resources.[35] Fast promotion for early recruits depended on a base that grew faster still. Not everyone wanted to climb. 'I don't have to become a project manager if I don't want to,' said Sushil, who worked in the company's mobile-commerce practice and is identified in the article only by his first name. 'I can focus on the technology and become a technical consultant to projects.'[36]

## The millennium bug

The work that filled the base of the pyramid in the late 1990s was Y2K. Rajaraman explains the problem simply. Programs written in the 1970s and 1980s, 'mostly in COBOL', stored the year as two digits to save memory, on the assumption that the first two were 19. When the year became 2000 they would give wrong results, and every such program had to be found and corrected. 'This bug fix was labour intensive. There were not enough software engineers in the USA and Europe to fix the bug and it had to be outsourced. This was a godsend opportunity to many fledgling software services companies in India.'[37]

At Infosys, the 1999 filing shows how quickly the work arrived. Y2K projects made up about 7.5 per cent of revenue in the year to March 1997 and 23.3 per cent in the year to March 1998.[38] In the nine months to December 1998 the share was 21.4 per cent.[39] The figure often repeated, that Y2K was 23 per cent of Infosys's revenue 'in 1997', comes from Rajaraman, who took it from an earlier history.[40] It is the same number: the company's fiscal year 1998 ran from April 1997 to March 1998. Y2K tripled as a share of the business in a single year and had already begun to shrink as a share by the end of 1998.

The company was frank with American investors about what kind of work this was. 'The high demand for these time-sensitive projects results in pricing and margins that are favorable to the Company,' the filing said. It expected demand to 'begin to diminish rapidly after fiscal 1999', and it could not promise to replace the work with other work at the same margins.[41] Then came a sentence about people. 'There is an additional risk that the Company may be unable to retrain and redeploy IT professionals who are currently assigned to Year 2000 conversion projects involving legacy computer systems after such projects are completed.'[42] In a document filed under American securities law, the leading Indian firm said that a wave of demand had trained a cohort of its engineers for work that would soon end, and that it might not find other work for them.

For the industry, the figures come from the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, as reported by the trade newsletter *Computergram* in June 1999. Indian software exports in FY1998-99 were $2.65 billion, up 51.4 per cent, and Y2K work accounted for $560 million of that, or 21.1 per cent. Nasscom said that 203 of the Fortune 1000 companies used Indian software services, and that 25 firms earned 63 per cent of all exports.[43] Two weeks earlier the same newsletter had reported a larger Nasscom estimate: that Indian firms had earned $2.3 billion from the bug, might reach $3 billion by the end of 1999, and would earn only 'a few hundred million dollars' from it the following year.[44] The cumulative figure is hard to reconcile with $560 million in the peak year unless it spans several years and other kinds of work. The share of a single year's exports, about a fifth, is the safer number. The same report described the trap that the end of the work would set. Large companies around the world, it said, were holding back from buying new computer systems until the millennium had passed, and were no longer spending much on the bug either, because most of it had been dealt with. Indian firms that had relied on Y2K feared that their profits would fall.[45]

Nasscom already had an answer to the end of the work. Its president, Dewang Mehta, spoke of 'three Es', electronic commerce, enterprise resource planning (ERP, the integrated software that large companies were then installing to run their accounts, stock and staff) and euro conversion, and of an export target of $50 billion by FY2007-08.[46] The euro was a second conversion job. The European Union announced in 1995 that the single currency would be used from 1 January 1999, and banks and other financial institutions had to change their programs before then. In Rajaraman's words, this 'was a labour intensive job and provided software conversion contracts to numerous Indian software companies'.[47] No figures for the value of euro work to Indian firms have been found.

The millennium arrived without a crisis. In early 2000 the news magazine *Outlook* asked in a headline whether the whole thing had been 'The Rs 1,800 Cr Hoax?'. It put the world's spending on the problem at $600 billion, about $150 billion of it in the United States. It reported Nasscom's estimate that Y2K preparations had cost India Rs 1,800 crore across government and private industry, of which Rs 600 crore was for software and services.[48] The magazine converted the total to $3.6 billion. At the 1999 average exchange rate it was about $420 million.[49] The article also recorded what the night had been like for the firms. Rajeev K. Arora, resident manager of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), a company that by the magazine's account had written more than 650 million lines of code for Y2K correction, said TCS had bought overseas tickets and arranged visas so that it could fly its engineers to clients if anything went wrong, and had stocked diesel for its generators.[50] Mehta's own verdict, as *Outlook* quoted it, was that 'Y2K was a godsend and might prove to be the turning point for the industry.'[51]

Was it the turning point? The export figures say not. In the series Rajaraman reproduces, Indian software exports had grown by between about a quarter and two-thirds a year in every year from 1990-91 to 1997-98 (Chapter 9 compares it with a second series), most of that before Y2K work became large.[52] At its peak Y2K was about a fifth of the industry's exports and about a fifth of the leading firm's revenue, and that firm expected it to fade quickly. What Y2K did, on the best evidence, was open doors. Rajaraman writes that many firms 'earned the goodwill of clients by not only fixing the Y2K bug but also improving the software (when appropriate) at no extra cost', and that 'This opportunity gave many software services companies entry to the Fortune 500 companies and enabled them to get software development contracts later.'[53] He also gives part of the credit for the quiet rollover to the programmers 'working diligently in India between 1993 and 1999'.[54] That is his judgement, and the *Outlook* article shows that it was not universally shared at the time.[55] The common belief that Y2K made the Indian industry is half right. It accelerated growth that had already begun, and it put Indian engineers inside the systems of large American companies, some of which kept them on for other work.

None of the engineers who did the Y2K work has left an account that this book has found. They appear in the record only as numbers in filings and as the 'IT professionals' whom Infosys feared it could not redeploy.

## Two hundred thousand applications

The engineers on the bus in 2000 had been chosen from a very large crowd. Chapter 9 followed the company's recruiting funnel in the year to March 1998, when about 70,870 applications produced about 1,300 joiners.[56] *Business Today* reported 183,966 applications in 1999 and 259,820 in 2000 up to 1 December, and 2,991 people hired in the six months from April to September 2000.[57] In the year to March 2002 the company received about 193,640 applications, interviewed about 6,730 people, made about 1,710 offers and saw about 1,550 accepted. It said it focused 'on the top 20% of students from engineering departments of Indian schools'.[58] About one applicant in 55 joined in 1997-98, and about one in 125 in 2001-02. These are the company's figures and it used them to advertise itself. They also show that the supply of engineering graduates who wanted these jobs was growing far faster than even the fastest-growing firm could take them. The national supply at the end of the decade, on the figures Saxenian took from Nasscom (Chapter 10), ran to tens of thousands of computer science graduates and hundreds of thousands of private trainees a year.[59] The leading firms did not depend on either. Infosys, which in 1991 had advertised for engineers of any discipline and promised to train them (Chapter 9), still selected by its own tests and taught its own methods.[60]

The firm explained its appeal in its own terms. In 1999 it told American investors that, because of its stock option plan, it had 'become one of the most sought after employers for Indian engineering graduates', with attrition 'significantly below the industry average'. It added that 'India is home to the world's second largest population of English-speaking technical talent'.[61] Both statements were the company's description of itself.

The education that mattered most happened after the degree, in the three-month course that every batch of new engineers took in the training centre the reporter had been shown.[62] Chapter 12 follows the company's training system as it grew, including its campus at Mysore (Mysuru since 2014). Taken with Rajaraman's account of process, this is the shape of the system that the next chapter follows at full scale. The firm selected from a vast pool, trained its recruits for three months in its own methods, and placed them into a documented process.

The people inside it were mostly engineers. The magazine counted 4,616 employees on the Bangalore campus in late 2000, and said that apart from the 840 people in the company's staff functions, such as human resources, finance, marketing and administration, everyone was an engineer.[63] The magazine noticed the strain as well as the perks. 'Every time things get a little too much for me,' said an employee who, it reported, 'not infrequently puts in 16 hours a day at work', 'I go out for a smoke, or a walk, or play a few holes of golf.' Muthamma Acharya, 'a twenty-something marketing executive', described the pace of hiring: 'You come in one morning and find the breakfast line 400-people longer'.[64] Suparna Shankar, an assistant manager in marketing for the Asia-Pacific region, summed up the place for the magazine: 'You can create a role for yourself.'[65] These were the voices a magazine chose for a story about the best employer in India. No account by an engineer who disliked the work, or left, has been found for this period.

## Nasdaq

Infosys had listed in India in 1993, in an offering Murthy remembered as 'a very tough time' (Chapter 9).[66] Six years later it went to New York. The final prospectus, dated 10 March 1999 and filed the next day, offered 1.8 million American Depositary Shares (ADSs), certificates traded in the United States that each represented half an Indian share, at $34.00 each. The offering raised $61.2 million before an underwriting discount of $1.68 a share. The shares were to be quoted on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol INFY.[67] On 10 March the equivalent price of the shares on the Mumbai exchange had been $37.18 per ADS, at Rs 42.50 to the dollar, so the American price was set a little below the Indian one. Until then, the prospectus noted, there had been no public market for the company's shares in the United States.[68] The company's press release, which this book could not obtain, is the source of the widely repeated claim that Infosys was the first Indian company to list on an American exchange, and the claim is not repeated here.

Murthy gave a specific reason for the listing. Infosys had prepared its accounts under American accounting rules voluntarily from 1995, so that clients could read them. 'Later on, we said, "Look. We have to create an employee stock option plan in the U.S. currency." Therefore, we wanted ADRs [American Depository Receipts], and that is how we got listed on NASDAQ in 1999.'[69] In his account, the listing was as much about paying staff as about raising money.

Others followed. In June 1999 Mehta of Nasscom said he expected up to ten Indian firms to list in the United States over the next twelve to eighteen months.[70] The next was not a software services firm but an internet company. Satyam Infoway, the internet subsidiary of Satyam Computer Services, priced its ADSs on 18 October 1999 at $4.50 each (the filing appears to give this on the basis it uses for its price history, after a four-for-one split of its ADSs in January 2000), and they began trading on Nasdaq the next day.[71] Satyam Computer Services owned about 52.5 per cent of it in 2002.[72] A rival Indian content provider, Rediff.com, completed its own American offering in June 2000.[73]

## Rupee millionaires

The listing turned paper into wealth for employees because Infosys had given them paper. 'In 1994, the Company established the ESOP, one of the first employee stock option plans in India,' the 1999 filing said. A trust set up for the purpose held warrants for shares, and employees received rights to buy shares at Rs 100 each, $2.35 at the exchange rate of February 1999, which the filing called 'substantially below the market price'. The rights vested over five years.[74] The filing explains the plan at length because under American accounting rules the discount was a cost, and under Indian rules it was not.[75] Stock options were so unusual in India that the government's information technology task force of 1998, among its 108 recommendations, proposed allowing 'sweat equity' and employee stock option plans, which Rajaraman describes as 'alien to other industries in India'. That required a change in company law.[76]

A rupee millionaire, in the magazine's count quoted at the start of this chapter, held at least Rs 10 lakh (Rs 1 million), about $22,000 at the 2000 exchange rate.[77] That was a large sum for an engineer in his or her twenties, but not a fortune. A dollar millionaire was another matter. Infosys's sales had grown from Rs 88.97 crore in the year to March 1996 to Rs 884.35 crore in the year to March 2000.[78] The new wealth reached the city. 'Indeed, a couple of enterprising Bangalore-based real-estate developers make a living primarily from selling apartments to people who work for Infosys,' the magazine wrote.[79] In 2020 Murthy put the scale of the programme in his own words: Infosys had distributed 19 per cent of its equity to employees through stock options, worth about $9 billion at that time's prices.[80] It is his figure.

The money was very unevenly spread. It went to those who had joined early, at the leading firm, and stayed long enough to vest. A graduate who joined a smaller firm, or who joined Infosys in 2001, was in a different position.

## The bust

The bust looked different depending on where one stood. For investors in Indian internet shares it was a collapse. Satyam Infoway's annual report for the year to March 2002 said that since the offering, and after the split, its ADSs had traded between 'a high of $113 per ADS' and a low of $0.87.[81] The price table in the same report shows a low of $0.72 in the quarter to September 2001.[82] On 5 November 2001 a securities class action was filed in New York on behalf of everyone who had bought its ADSs between 20 October 1999 and 6 December 2000. It named the company, some of its executives and some of the underwriters of its offering, and alleged that the underwriters had failed to disclose commissions and arrangements with investors to whom they allocated shares.[83] In October 2001 Satyam Computer Services announced that it intended to sell its shares in the company.[84] The parent's own later history belongs to Chapter 16.

For the largest services firm the bust was a slower line, not a fall. From the year to March 1998 to the year to March 2002, Infosys's revenue grew at a compound 68.1 per cent a year and its IT staff rose from about 2,200 to about 9,400.[85] But its outlook for the following year was cautious. 'The economic slowdown in the U.S. has impacted the growth prospects of companies that are in the insurance, banking and financial services and telecom segments,' it said, and companies 'may cut their IT spending or postpone decisions regarding new IT expenditures'.[86] The industry's exports kept rising. The Reserve Bank of India recorded software services receipts of $6.3 billion in the year to March 2001 and $7.6 billion in the year to March 2002.[87]

For new graduates, the bust arrived on campus. In January 2002 *The Hindu Business Line* reported that Anna University had placed 'only around 320 students with various companies, down from 1,200 around the same time last year'. The year before had been a record: 65 per cent of the 70 companies that visited the university had been IT firms. This time about 35 companies came. Wipro and Satyam, which had taken 49 and 23 students the year before, did not come at all. TCS recruited 54 students against 177, Infosys 46 against 126, and Cognizant Technology Solutions 69 against 105.[88] Dr N. Baluswamy, who directed the university's Centre for University-Industry Collaboration, which ran placements, said that some of the previous year's graduates had seen their offers postponed indefinitely, and that the centre had negotiated with the companies. 'A few companies have delayed the date of joining for last year students by over a year,' he said. Some IT companies, 'except big players such as TCS, Infosys and CTS', had cut the pay promised on campus 'by 50-60 per cent'.[89]

At the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) in Madras (Chennai since 1996), a little over 400 of the 719 students registered with the placement centre had been recruited by 51 companies, 30 of them in IT, with ten companies still to come, against about 750 placed the year before. About 30 per cent of students stayed away from campus interviews that year, the paper reported, because of 'shocking stories of lay-offs, delayed appointments and salary cuts' among the previous year's recruits. Most engineering students now wanted 'to consider only engineering companies, rather than shift to IT', and some said they wanted stable jobs.[90] Companies from outside IT were coming back. Maruti Udyog returned after about four years and the Gas Authority of India after fifteen, and NTPC was expected for the first time. At a management institute in Tiruchi, the highest offer came from Citibank, at Rs 6.5 lakh a year, about $13,600.[91]

The pattern matters for the rest of this book. In the placement director's account, the largest firms did not cut the pay they had promised; other firms cut salaries, and some put off joining dates by more than a year. The colleges went on producing graduates while the firms at the end of the pipeline cut their campus intake, the two largest at Anna University by more than half. No graduate whose joining was deferred in 2001-02 has been found speaking in their own words; they appear only through a placement director's account. Later chapters show the same pattern returning.

## Hours and outcomes

One thread runs through the filings of these years and connects them to the end of this book. Chapter 9 showed that most of Infosys's revenue in the mid-1990s came from time-and-materials contracts, under which the client pays for the hours or months worked, and that by 1999 the company said it wanted more fixed-price work.[92] Y2K added a lesson of its own. It paid well because it was urgent: the company said that 'high demand for these time-sensitive projects' brought favourable prices and margins.[93] The risk ran the other way too: the 1999 filing counted 'the accuracy of estimates of resources and time required to complete ongoing projects, particularly projects performed under fixed-price, fixed-time frame contracts' among the causes of uneven results.[94] Under a fixed price, a project that overran cost the firm and not the client.

By 2002 the company reported progress. 'As compare to the previous year, we have increased the proportion of projects that are undertaken on a fixed-price, fixed-timeframe, rather than a time-and-material basis, which reduce client risk, and if effectively structured and executed, provide opportunities for enhanced margins.'[95] A firm that sells hours earns less when its engineers work faster, unless it uses the saving to win more work. A firm that sells an outcome at a fixed price keeps what it saves. Before 2002 the leading Indian firm had decided that it wanted, where it could, to sell outcomes. When tools arrive that cut the hours needed for coding and testing, the work that Rajaraman says took 70 to 80 per cent of a project's time and was done in India, the way a contract is priced decides who keeps the gain.[96]

In 2002 that question was still far off. The more immediate change was in the size of the machine. In 1991 Infosys had advertised for sixty-four engineers.[97] In 2002 it employed about 10,740 people and had received nearly 200,000 applications in a year.[98] The firms' demand for new engineers had fallen for a season. The supply had not. The next chapter follows the graduates who kept coming, and the companies that learned to hire them by the thousand.
